newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE - Morocco tries to cut carnage on notorious roads.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Morocco tries to cut carnage on notorious roads.

text.p: Morocco is taking a hard look at its drivers and their vehicles to tackle what one frightened motorist complained was "civil war on the roads".
That "civil war" in the first six months of last year saw 1,196 people killed and 26,599 injured in 18,033 traffic accidents.
And that was an improvement on the previous year. In the same period of 1995, road accidents claimed 1,618 lives and injured more than 30,000.
Morocco's authorities agree the roads are scary and want to cut the number of accidents by 30 per cent by the year 2000.
Stepping into a row over higher insurance premiums, Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj said the country had nine times more accidents than France and 10 times more than Norway.

The increased insurance rates sparked a two-week strike by taxi drivers, whose distinctly coloured "petits (small) taxis" appear to many casual observers to show little regard for the rules of the road.
Taking the bus may be no safer.
Last month, 23 bus passengers were swept away by floods when the driver failed to notice a road diversion sign south of Rabat.

Under a headline "Madness at the Wheel", the Moroccan Transport Magazine lamented: "Lack of safety on the road has become one of the greatest social plagues of our time, one of the most agonising problems modern life inflicts on society."
One despairing motorist quoted by the newspaper L'Opinion described it thus: "There's civil war on the roads."
WORST ACCIDENT RATE

With only 1.166 million cars on the roads in 1995 for a country of 27 million people, Morocco topped the international list of accident rates compiled by the National Committee for the Prevention of Road Accidents, logging 41,552.
It was far ahead of neighbouring Algeria, which reported 24,842 accidents for 2.1 million cars.
Moroccan efforts to cut the toll are starting to work.

"There was a five percent reduction in the number of accidents in 1995 after the government said it considered it as its top priority," said Driss Lasfar, Permanent Secretary at the National Committee for the Prevention of Road Accidents.
"Anti-accident campaigns and particularly fines up to 400 dirhams ($44) for excessive speed have had a deterrent effect on drivers," Lasfar added.
Up to 1994, fines used to range from 10 dirhams for light violations to 35 dirhams for more serious ones.
Many experts blame a combination of factors for the high accident rate - bad drivers, old cars, and "black spots" on the roads.
Would-be drivers are now finding it tougher to get licences. Only 63 percent passed their tests in 1996 compared to 95 percent the year before.
From the age of 18 Moroccans can get a driving permit after paying 2,000 dirhams ($220) for about one month's training. It includes a test on the highway code and one behind the wheel.
Vigilance committees in all provinces now pay surprise visits to driving schools to check whether they are complying with the rules.
"BLACK SPOTS" LISTED

Efforts to improve notorious accident spots are being made by the roads body Direction des Routes. It lists a total of 379 black spots -- where at least 10 accidents and 10 deaths or serious injuries have occurred in five years.
Accidents are expensive. In 1995, they cost the country more than one billion dirhams ($109 million), according to the National Committee for the Prevention of Road Accidents.
The "old car" factor is also being looked at.
Lasfar said that most cars on the road were second-hand and came from Europe.
But last year about 15,000 new "economic cars" helped cut the average age. These new cars launched by Italy's Fiat in 1995 are sold at reduced prices.
A new law is being studied to require mechanical inspections for cars after five years, instead of 10 years as at present.
With about 55 percent of Morocco population illiterate, the government is preparing a booklet and audio-visual material to make them aware of road dangers.
"Some people find it difficult to realise they are reponsible of other people's lives especially if they have not been to school," Lasfar said.
"There is a combination of the human factor, the state of the vehicle and the road infrastructure in a accident, but the human element remains able to make the balance swing one way or another."
